picks.style: greek threnody, lyre over low drone, single male voice, austere, funereal, very slow
picks.why: The great pessimist chorus of Greek verse — mourn the newborn, send out the dead rejoicing, men as generations of leaves.

picks.style: orphic hymn, kithara and hand drums, layered male voices, rolling, majestic, building
picks.why: 'Lord of aether and Hades, of sea and earth' — a hymn with a seasonal turn: yours the spring of purple flowers, yours the winter.

picks.style: mystic hymn, aulos and finger cymbals, ecstatic tenor over drone, rising, luminous
picks.why: Souls of the pious singing hymns in heaven, and the poet with golden wings and the sandals of the Sirens going up into the aether.

picks.style: urdu nazm, sitar and harmonium, soft tabla, warm male vocal, contemplative, slow, night-lit
picks.why: The Assembly of Stars — the sun pelting evening with tulips from the platter of the horizon, then the angel's call to the night-watchers.

picks.style: qawwali, harmonium, tabla and dholak, handclaps, impassioned lead with chorus responses, driving, defiant
picks.why: The Shikwa's complaint to God — 'Forgive the words, but You are fickle in Your worldly ways' — question after question, made for call and response.

picks.style: melancholy urdu ghazal, harmonium and sarangi, plaintive male vocal, rubato, intimate
picks.why: The garden after the roses: songbirds flown, branches stripped, one lone nightingale still carrying a tempest of melody.

picks.style: georgian winter song, harpsichord and viols, baritone, sparse, cold, slow
picks.why: The Winter's Walk — naked hill, leafless grove, hoary ground — clean quatrains where the season takes over the heart.

picks.style: augustan ode, martial drums and brass, declamatory baritone with chorus, stately, building
picks.why: Charles XII: 'Think nothing gain'd, he cries, till nought remain' — Famine guarding the coast, Winter barricading the realm of Frost.

picks.style: 18th century satirical ballad, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy, wry male voice, brisk, biting
picks.why: 'Slow rises worth, by poverty depress'd' — the line everyone quotes from London, in its own street-noise setting.

picks.style: roman comic cantica, tibia pipes and lyre, wry baritone patter, brisk, chamber
picks.why: Davus on the unfairness of gifts — what the poor man spares ounce by ounce is carried off by the rich without a thought.

picks.style: roman stage song, tibia and soft strings, tender tenor, gentle, unhurried
picks.why: The girl weeping over her dead mother with no one but one old woman to help her bury her — the play's one moment of real feeling.

picks.style: balinese sacred chant, gamelan metallophones and bamboo flute, low male chant over drone, slow, ceremonial
picks.why: The four states — dream like foam and bubbles, deep sleep a thicket of darkness — closing on ghee hidden in milk.

picks.style: kawi recitation, suling flute and gong, two voices in question and answer, measured, reverent
picks.why: Śiva on Kailāsa opening the teaching, with the blind men groping at the elephant and misleading one another.

picks.style: sanskrit-kawi litany, drone and small gongs, unison male chant, hypnotic, steady
picks.why: Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, imperishable — a litany of epithets that is already a chant.

picks.style: latin love lyric, kithara and reed pipe, warm tenor, tender, flowing, moderate
picks.why: Garlands for the birthday and songs for the guardian spirit — flowers traded for kisses, ending where the reed-pipe outsings the poet.

picks.style: roman light verse, plucked lyre and hand drum, playful tenor, witty, brisk, chamber
picks.why: The tooth-powder poem — a fine white noble little powder, so no grime shows if you should happen to smile.

picks.style: victorian recitative song, piano and strings, sober baritone, restrained, slow
picks.why: Only candidate; it opens on a line worth singing — 'Fame bears no fruit till the vain planter dies'.

picks.style: oracular chant, sparse aulos and struck bowl, single grave voice over drone, hushed, very slow
picks.why: Only candidate; the Sibylline warning about the king of Egypt reads as oracle and carries the right menace.
